Flour dust settled like frost over the stainless-steel prep table. At 3:15 a.m., Arthur found the book. It sat beside the sourdough starter, exactly where he had found a different library volume every Thursday for a month. 

Tonight’s book was a battered copy of *The Birds of eastern North America*. Arthur picked it up, leaving a white thumbprint on the fabric spine. The library stamp on the pocket inside showed it was three weeks overdue. 

He flipped the pages. A slip of blue lined paper fluttered out onto the floury table. 

*The yeast in my kitchen won’t rise,* the pencil handwriting read. *I am trying your method. Page 112.*

Arthur turned to page 112. The margins were clean, but someone had pressed a single, dried hop blossom flat against the illustration of a cedar waxwing. 

Arthur smelled the paper. It carried the faint, bitter scent of wild fermentation, not the sterile scent of the library. He tucked the note into his apron pocket. He walked to the back of the kitchen, scooped a cup of active, bubbling rye starter into a clean glass jar, and pressed a square of cheesecloth over the lid with a rubber band.
